title: Rainbows and the Colors of Light
summary: How sunlight bends and reflects inside raindrops to split white light into the colors of a rainbow, and when and where to see one.
poll: Rainbows are easy to explain with science.

versions.title: A Bow in the Sky
versions.text:
The rain stops. The sun comes out. Look up! You may see a big bow of bright bands. It is a rainbow.

Sunlight looks white. But it is not one hue. It is a mix of hues. Each hue is a color.

Rain hangs in the air in tiny drops. A raindrop is like a small glass ball. Light goes in. It bends. It hits the back. It bounces. It bends once more on the way out.

Each color bends a bit more or less. So the colors split up. They make an arc.

The bands are in the same order. Red is on top. Then come orange, yellow, and green. Then come blue and indigo. Violet is at the bottom.

The sun must be at your back. The rain must be in front of you. Look when the sun is low.

Some days you see two bows. The top bow is pale. Its colors are flipped.

A clear glass block can split light, too. It is a prism. Long ago, Ibn al-Haytham and then Isaac Newton studied light.

You can make a rainbow at home. Put the sun at your back. Spray a hose. Look for the arc!

versions.title: A Bow in the Sky
versions.text:
The rain stops, and the sun comes out. Look up! You may see a big bow of bright stripes. It is a rainbow.

Sunlight looks white to us. But it is not one color. It is a mix of many colors.

After rain, tiny drops of water float in the air. Each raindrop is like a small, round glass ball. Sunlight goes in, and it bends. It bounces off the back of the drop. Then it bends once more on the way out.

Each color bends by a different amount. So the colors spread out. They make a curved line called an arc.

The colors are in the same order each time. Red is on the top. Then come orange, yellow, green, blue, and indigo. Violet is at the bottom.

To see a rainbow, the sun must be behind you. The rain must be in front of you. The best time is when the sun is low.

Some days you can see two bows. The top one is not as bright. Its colors are in the back to front order.

A clear glass block called a prism can split light too. Long ago, Ibn al-Haytham and then Isaac Newton studied light.

You can make your own rainbow. Stand with the sun behind you. Spray water from a hose. Look for the arc!

versions.title: Rainbows: Light in the Sky
versions.text:
The rain has stopped. The sun peeks out from the clouds. Look up, and you may see a bright band of colors. It is a rainbow. It is made of sunlight and water.

Sunlight looks white. But it is really a mix of many colors. We do not see them until something splits them apart.

After rain, lots of tiny raindrops float in the air. Each one works like a small glass ball. When sunlight goes into a drop, the light bends. It bounces off the back of the drop. Then it bends again as it leaves.

Each color bends a little more or a little less. That is why the colors spread out. They make a curved shape called an arc.

The colors are always in the same order. Red is on the outside of the arc. Next come orange, yellow, green, blue, and indigo. Violet is on the inside.

To see a rainbow, stand with the sun behind you and the rain in front of you. It is best to look in the morning or late in the day, when the sun is low.

Sometimes there is a second rainbow above the first. It is not as bright, and its colors are in the opposite order.

A clear glass block called a prism can split light into colors too. Ibn al-Haytham studied light about a thousand years ago. Later, Isaac Newton used a prism to show that white light holds many colors.

You can make a rainbow yourself. On a sunny day, stand with the sun behind you. Then spray a fine mist from a hose.

versions.title: Rainbows: Light in the Sky
versions.text:
When a rain shower ends and the sun breaks through the clouds, a bright band of colors may curve across the sky. This is a rainbow. It may look like magic, but it is made of two plain things: sunlight and water.

Sunlight looks white, but it is a mixture of many colors. We do not usually see them, because they travel together.

After rain, lots of tiny raindrops hang in the air. Each raindrop acts like a small, round glass ball. When sunlight enters a drop, the light bends. Then it reflects, or bounces, off the back of the drop. Last, it bends again as it leaves.

Each color bends by a slightly different amount. So the colors split up and spread out into a curved shape called an arc.

The colors are always in the same order. Red is on the outside of the arc. Then come orange, yellow, green, blue, and indigo. Violet is on the inside.

To see a rainbow, you must stand with the sun behind you and the rain in front of you. Rainbows are seen most in the morning or late in the day, when the sun is low in the sky.

Sometimes a second rainbow forms above the first one. It is not as bright, and its colors are in the reverse order.

A prism, a clear block of glass, can also split light into colors. Ibn al-Haytham studied light about a thousand years ago. Many years later, Isaac Newton used prisms to prove that white light holds all the colors.

You can even make your own rainbow. On a sunny day, stand with the sun behind you and spray a fine mist from a garden hose.

versions.title: Rainbows and the Colors of Light
versions.text:
When a rain shower ends and the sun breaks through the clouds, a curved band of colors sometimes stretches across the sky. People have loved rainbows for thousands of years. The science behind them needs just two everyday things: sunlight and water.

Sunlight looks white, but it is really a mixture of many colors. Scientists call this full range of colors the spectrum. We do not usually see the separate colors, because they travel together in one beam.

After rain, millions of tiny raindrops float in the air, and each one acts like a small glass ball. When sunlight enters a drop, it slows down and bends. This bending is called refraction. The light then reflects off the back of the drop. It bends a second time as it leaves.

Each color bends by a slightly different amount, so the colors split apart and fan out into a curved arc. Red is always on the outside. Then come orange, yellow, green, blue, and indigo, with violet on the inside.

Every observer must stand with the sun behind them and the rain in front of them. Rainbows show up most in the morning or late afternoon, when the sun is low in the sky.

Sometimes a second, fainter rainbow forms above the first. Light reflects twice inside the drops, so its colors are in the reverse order.

A prism, a clear block of glass, also splits light into the spectrum. Ibn al-Haytham studied light about a thousand years ago. Later, Isaac Newton used prisms to prove that white light holds every color.

You can make a rainbow yourself. Stand with the sun behind you and spray a fine mist from a garden hose.

versions.title: Rainbows and the Colors of Light
versions.text:
When a rain shower ends and the sun emerges from behind the clouds, a curved band of colors occasionally stretches across the sky. People have admired rainbows for thousands of years. The scientific explanation for them depends on only two ordinary ingredients: sunlight and water.

Although sunlight appears white, it is actually a mixture of many different colors. Scientists call this complete range of colors the visible spectrum. Normally we cannot distinguish the separate colors, because they travel together in a single beam.

After rain, millions of tiny raindrops remain suspended in the atmosphere, and each one behaves like a miniature glass sphere. When sunlight enters a drop, it slows down and changes direction, a process called refraction. The light then reflects off the back of the drop. It bends a second time as it exits into the air.

Because each color bends by a slightly different amount, the colors gradually separate and fan out into a curved arc. Red always appears on the outside, followed by orange, yellow, green, blue, and indigo, with violet on the inside.

An observer can see a rainbow only when the sun is behind them and the falling rain is in front of them. Consequently, rainbows appear most frequently in the morning or late afternoon, when the sun is positioned low in the sky.

Occasionally, a second, fainter rainbow develops above the first. Because the light reflects twice inside each drop, its colors appear in reverse order.

A prism, a transparent block of glass, can also separate light into the spectrum. Ibn al-Haytham carefully investigated light about a thousand years ago, and centuries later Isaac Newton used prisms to demonstrate that white light contains every color.

You can create a rainbow yourself by standing with the sun behind you and spraying a fine mist from a garden hose.

versions.title: Rainbows and the Colors of Light
versions.text:
When a rain shower ends and the sun emerges from behind the retreating clouds, a curved band of brilliant colors occasionally stretches across the sky. People in many civilizations have admired rainbows for thousands of years. Yet the scientific explanation for this beautiful sight depends on only two ordinary ingredients, sunlight and water.

Although sunlight appears white, it is actually a combination of many different colors, which scientists describe as the visible spectrum. Each color is light with a different wavelength, the distance between the peaks of its waves. Red has the longest wavelength, while violet has the shortest. Normally we cannot distinguish these colors, because they travel together in a single beam.

After rain, millions of tiny raindrops remain suspended in the atmosphere, and each one behaves like a miniature glass sphere. When sunlight enters a drop, it slows down and changes direction, a process known as refraction. The light then undergoes reflection off the back of the drop. It bends a second time as it exits into the surrounding air.

Because each wavelength bends by a slightly different amount, the colors gradually separate and fan out into a curved arc, an effect called dispersion. Red, which bends the least, consistently appears on the outside, followed by orange, yellow, green, blue, and indigo, while violet, which bends the most, appears on the inside.

An observer can see this phenomenon only when the sun is behind them and the falling rain is in front of them. As a result, rainbows appear most frequently in the early morning or late afternoon, when the sun is low in the sky.

Occasionally, a second, fainter rainbow develops above the first. Because the light reflects twice inside each drop, its colors appear in reverse order.

A prism, a transparent block of glass, produces the same dispersion of light into the spectrum. Ibn al-Haytham systematically investigated light approximately a thousand years ago, and centuries later Isaac Newton used prisms to demonstrate that white light contains every color.

You can create a rainbow yourself by standing with the sun behind you and spraying a fine mist from a garden hose.

versions.title: Rainbows and the Colors of Light
versions.text:
When a rain shower concludes and the sun emerges from behind the retreating clouds, a curved band of brilliant colors occasionally stretches across the sky. Numerous civilizations have admired rainbows for thousands of years, yet the scientific explanation for this remarkable atmospheric phenomenon depends on only two ordinary ingredients, sunlight and water.

Although sunlight appears white, it is actually a combination of many different colors, which scientists collectively describe as the visible spectrum. Each color corresponds to light of a particular wavelength, meaning the distance between successive peaks of its electromagnetic waves, and red possesses the longest wavelength while violet possesses the shortest. Ordinarily we cannot distinguish these individual colors, because they travel together in a single, apparently colorless beam.

After rainfall, millions of tiny raindrops remain suspended in the atmosphere, and each one functions like a miniature transparent sphere. When sunlight penetrates a drop, it decelerates and changes direction, a process known as refraction. The light subsequently undergoes reflection off the interior surface at the back of the drop, and it refracts a second time as it exits into the surrounding air.

Because each wavelength refracts by a slightly different amount, the colors progressively separate and fan out into a curved arc, an effect physicists call dispersion. Red, which bends the least, consistently appears on the outside, followed by orange, yellow, green, blue, and indigo, while violet, which bends the most, appears on the innermost edge.

An observer can witness this phenomenon only when the sun is positioned directly behind them and the precipitation is in front of them, which explains why rainbows materialize most frequently in the early morning or late afternoon, when the sun is relatively low on the horizon.

Occasionally, a secondary, fainter rainbow develops above the primary one, and because the light reflects twice inside each droplet before emerging, its colors appear in reverse order.

A prism, a transparent block of glass, produces an identical dispersion of light into the spectrum. Ibn al-Haytham systematically investigated the behavior of light approximately a thousand years ago, and centuries afterward Isaac Newton employed prisms to demonstrate conclusively that ordinary white light contains every color.

You can generate a miniature rainbow yourself by standing with the sun behind you and spraying a fine mist from a garden hose.

keyWords.definition: the light that comes from the sun
keyWords.example: Sunlight came through the window and warmed the room.
A raindrop landed on my nose.

keyWords.definition: to change direction or shape so it is not straight
keyWords.example: The road bends to the left near the park.

keyWords.definition: a curved line, like part of a circle
keyWords.example: The ball flew through the air in a high arc.

keyWords.definition: a clear block of glass that splits light into colors
keyWords.example: Our teacher held a prism in the sun, and colors appeared on the wall.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: Why rain falls from the clouds in the sky
How sunlight and raindrops make a rainbow
How to paint a picture of a rainbow
Why the sun is hot
questions.why: Most of the article explains how sunlight bends inside raindrops and splits into the colors of a rainbow.

wrong.A: The article talks about rain, but not about why it falls.
wrong.C: The article does not talk about painting.
wrong.D: The article does not explain why the sun is hot.

questions.stem: What is sunlight really made of?
options: A mix of many colors
Only bright yellow light
Tiny drops of rain water
Clear glass
questions.why: The article says sunlight looks white but is a mix of many colors.

wrong.B: Sunlight holds many colors, not just yellow.
wrong.C: Raindrops are in the air, but sunlight is not made of water.
wrong.D: A prism is made of glass. Sunlight is not.

questions.stem: Where must the sun be for you to see a rainbow?
options: In front of you
Right above your head
Behind the clouds
Behind you
questions.why: The article says the sun must be behind you (at your back) and the rain in front of you.

wrong.A: The rain should be in front of you, not the sun.
wrong.B: The article says it is best when the sun is low, not high above you.
wrong.C: A rainbow needs sunlight to shine on the rain, so the sun cannot be hidden.

questions.stem: The article says the colors of a rainbow make an arc. What is an arc?
options: A small drop of water
A bright light at night
A curved line or shape
A straight line
questions.why: The article calls the arc a curved line or curved shape, like the bow of a rainbow.

wrong.A: A small drop of water is a raindrop.
wrong.B: The article does not use arc to mean a light at night.
wrong.D: An arc is curved, not straight.

questions.stem: Why do the colors of sunlight split apart inside a raindrop?
options: Each color bends by a different amount.
The raindrop is full of paint.
The wind blows the colors away.
The sun is very far away from the rain.
questions.why: The article explains that each color bends a little more or less, so the colors spread out.

wrong.C: The article does not say the wind splits the colors.
wrong.D: The sun is far away, but that is not why the colors split.

questions.stem: Why is it harder to see a rainbow at noon?
options: Raindrops dry up at noon.
There is no sunlight at noon.
Rainbows only come out late at night.
The sun is high in the sky, not low.
questions.why: The article says the best time is when the sun is low, in the morning or late in the day. At noon the sun is high.

wrong.A: The article does not say raindrops dry up at noon.
wrong.B: There is plenty of sunlight at noon.
wrong.C: Rainbows need sunlight, so they do not come at night.

questions.stem: Sara sprays a hose while facing the sun. She sees no rainbow. What should she do?
options: Spray the water up higher
Turn around so the sun is behind her
Wait until the sky gets dark at night
Use hot water instead
questions.why: The article says you must stand with the sun behind you to see a rainbow.

wrong.A: Spraying higher will not help if she is still facing the sun.
wrong.C: A rainbow needs sunlight, so the dark will not help.
wrong.D: The article does not say the water must be hot.

questions.stem: Why does the author tell about the hose at the end of the article?
options: To warn readers not to play with water
To explain why plants in a garden need lots of water
To show that readers can make a rainbow themselves
To tell a funny story
questions.why: The last part tells readers how to make their own rainbow with a hose and the sun behind them.

wrong.A: The author invites readers to try it, not to stay away from water.
wrong.B: The article does not talk about plants.
wrong.D: The ending gives steps to try, not a funny story.

checklist: I explained what happens to sunlight inside a raindrop.
I used at least two details from the article.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the article?

Isaac Newton was the very first person to ever see a rainbow.

questions.why: The article's main explanation is how raindrops bend and reflect sunlight so the colors of white light separate into a rainbow.

wrong.A: The article never says rainbows appear only in deserts.
wrong.B: Newton studied light with prisms. The article does not say he was the first to see a rainbow.
wrong.D: The hose is only a small activity at the end.

questions.stem: What is the bending of light called?
options: Refraction
Reflection
Spectrum
Mixture
questions.why: The article says that when sunlight enters a drop it slows and bends, and this bending is called refraction.

wrong.B: Reflection is when light bounces off the back of the drop.
wrong.C: The spectrum is the range of colors, not the bending.
wrong.D: Sunlight is a mixture of colors, but mixture is not the name for bending.

questions.stem: Which color appears on the inside of a rainbow?
options: Red
Orange
Green
Violet
questions.why: The article lists the colors from red on the outside to violet on the inside.

wrong.B: Orange is next to red, near the outside.
wrong.C: Green is in the middle of the rainbow.

questions.stem: The article says scientists call the full range of colors in sunlight the spectrum. What does spectrum mean?
options: A clear block of glass
The whole set of colors in light
A second rainbow that is fainter than the first
The back of a raindrop
questions.why: The article explains that the spectrum is the full range of colors that make up white light.

wrong.A: A clear block of glass is a prism.
wrong.C: A fainter rainbow is a second rainbow, not the spectrum.
wrong.D: The back of the drop is where light reflects.

questions.stem: Why are the colors of a second rainbow in reverse order?
options: The sun moves very quickly.
The second rainbow is made of different water.
The light reflects twice inside the drops.
The observer is standing on a hill.
questions.why: The article says light reflects twice inside the drops, so the second rainbow's colors appear in reverse order.

wrong.A: The article does not connect the order to how fast the sun moves.
wrong.B: Both rainbows come from the same raindrops.
wrong.D: The article does not mention hills.

questions.stem: At five o'clock in the afternoon, the sun is low in the west and rain is falling to the east. What can you infer?
options: Someone facing east has a good chance of seeing a rainbow.
No rainbow can form because it is too late.
Someone facing west will see a rainbow right around the setting sun.
The rain will turn into a prism.
questions.why: The sun is low and behind someone facing east, with rain in front of them, which matches the conditions in the article.

wrong.B: The article says late afternoon is one of the best times.
wrong.C: Facing west means looking toward the sun, but the sun must be behind you.
wrong.D: Rain does not turn into glass. A prism is a glass block.

questions.stem: What can you infer about a raindrop and a prism?
options: Both are made of glass.
Both make light brighter.
Both work only at night, when the sun is gone.
Both can bend light and split it into colors.
questions.why: The article says a raindrop acts like a small glass ball and a prism also splits light into the spectrum, so both bend light and separate colors.

wrong.A: A raindrop is water. It only acts like glass.
wrong.B: The article says they split light, not that they make it brighter.
wrong.C: Both need light, so they cannot work in the dark.

questions.stem: How does the author mainly explain how a rainbow forms?
options: By comparing rainbows in different countries
By describing, step by step, what light does inside a raindrop
By listing problems and their solutions
By telling a long story about one famous scientist's whole life

wrong.A: The article does not compare countries.
wrong.C: The article does not set up problems and solutions.

wrong.B: Raindrops only behave like glass spheres; they are water.
wrong.D: The article says violet bends the most, not less than red.

questions.stem: In the article, dispersion is described as an effect. Which meaning of dispersion fits the article?
options: The separation of light into its different colors
The reflection of light off a mirror
The evaporation of raindrops in sunlight
The slow movement of clouds across the sky after a heavy rain shower
questions.why: The article uses dispersion for the way the colors separate and fan out into an arc because each wavelength bends differently.

wrong.B: Reflection is a different step; dispersion is the spreading of colors.
wrong.C: The article does not discuss evaporation.
wrong.D: Clouds are mentioned only at the start, not as dispersion.

questions.stem: Why does red appear on the outside of the rainbow?
options: Red light travels in a separate beam from the sun.
Red reflects twice inside each drop.
Red has the shortest wavelength.
Red bends the least as it passes through the drop.
questions.why: The article explains that red, which bends the least, appears on the outside, while violet, which bends the most, appears on the inside.

wrong.A: The article says all colors travel together in one beam.
wrong.B: Reflecting twice explains the second rainbow, not red's position.
wrong.C: Red has the longest wavelength, not the shortest.

questions.stem: Based on the article, why might a person fail to see a rainbow during a summer shower at noon?
options: Raindrops are too large at noon.
Ibn al-Haytham proved that rainbows can never form in the middle of the day.
The sun is high, so it is not low behind the observer.
Sunlight contains no colors at midday.
questions.why: The article says rainbows appear most often when the sun is low behind the observer; at noon the sun is high overhead.

wrong.A: The article says nothing about the size of raindrops at noon.
wrong.B: The article does not say Ibn al-Haytham made this claim.
wrong.D: Sunlight always contains the full spectrum.

questions.stem: What would most likely happen if every color bent by exactly the same amount in a raindrop?
options: The colors would not separate, so no band of colors would appear.
The rainbow would become much brighter and wider than before.
Only a second, fainter rainbow would appear above the first.
The colors would appear in reverse order.
questions.why: The article says the colors separate because each wavelength bends by a different amount, so equal bending would keep them together as white light.

wrong.B: Without separation there would be no colored bands at all, not a brighter rainbow.
wrong.C: The second rainbow is caused by two reflections, not by equal bending.
wrong.D: Reverse order comes from two reflections, not equal bending.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention Ibn al-Haytham and Isaac Newton?
options: To argue that only famous people can study science
To show that scientists over many centuries studied light
To explain how to build a prism at home
To compare the countries where these two scientists lived and worked
questions.why: The author names scientists from different times to show that understanding light and color was built through careful study over centuries.

wrong.A: The article invites readers to try a rainbow experiment themselves.
wrong.C: The article does not explain how to build a prism.
wrong.D: The article does not compare their countries.

HIGH.prompt: Explain why a rainbow's colors always appear in the same order. Use evidence about wavelength, refraction, and dispersion from the article.
checklist: I explained the order of the colors with a clear claim.
I used at least two pieces of scientific evidence from the article.
I used the key words correctly.
